samples.text:
Many cities have old centres with beautiful buildings and long history. Some people think the government should not allow any new buildings in these areas, even if it is bad for economy and housing. I agree with this opinion to a large extent.

Firstly, historic city centres are very important for a country's culture and identity. Old buildings like churches, markets and palaces show how people lived in the past and they are part of our heritage. If the government allow modern buildings there, the old character of the area will be destroyed and we can never get it back. For example, a tall glass tower next to an old castle looks very strange and it make the area less beautiful.

Secondly, historic centres attract a lot of tourists. Tourists come to see the old streets and traditional architecture, not modern offices. So protecting these areas can actually help the economy, because tourism creates many jobs in hotels, restaurants and shops. In this way, the economic loss from not building is not so big as people think.

On the other hand, I understand that cities need more houses because the population is growing. Young people cannot find apartments with cheap price in the centre. However, I think new houses can be built in other parts of city, such as suburbs, where there are more space and the land is cheaper. The government can also improve public transport so people can travel to the centre easily.

In conclusion, I believe the government should stop new construction in historic city centres because these areas are very valuable for culture and tourism. The need for housing and economic growth can be solved in other areas of the city.
samples.why: Position clear though somewhat simplistic · relevant ideas with limited development · paragraphing appropriate · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary with some awkward collocations · several article and agreement errors.

samples.text:
In many cities, there is tension between preserving historic centres and meeting the demand for economic development and new housing. Some argue that governments should ban all new construction in these areas, whatever the economic cost. I agree that historic centres deserve strong protection, but I believe a complete ban goes too far.

There are strong reasons to protect historic districts. Their architecture represents centuries of cultural history, and once an old building is demolished or overshadowed by a modern tower, the loss is permanent. These areas also give cities a distinctive identity, which is valued by residents and is a major attraction for the tourists. In many European and Asian cities, the old town is the main reason visitors come at all, so careless development could damage the local economy rather than help it.

However, an absolute ban would create serious problems. City centres are usually where jobs, transport and services are concentrated, and preventing all new building there would push housing further from workplaces, increasing commuting times and rents. It might also turn historic districts into museum-like spaces, full of tourists but empty of ordinary residents and local businesses. A living city needs schools, shops and homes, not only monuments.

A more balanced solution is strict but flexible regulation. Governments can limit the height and design of new buildings so that they fit the character of the area, protect the most important landmarks completely, and encourage the conversion of old, empty buildings into housing. Many cities have successfully added modern homes on vacant plots without harming their historic appearance.

In conclusion, while historic city centres should be carefully protected, I disagree with preventing all new construction. Carefully controlled development can preserve heritage while still allowing cities to meet the needs of the people who live in them.
samples.why: Clear, balanced position maintained · ideas extended and supported, with occasional over-generalisation · logical progression and clear paragraph topics · good cohesion · some less common vocabulary · frequent error-free sentences.

samples.text:
Historic city centres are among the most visible expressions of a society's past, and the pressure to redevelop them is often intense. The proposal that governments should forbid all new construction in these districts, regardless of the economic and housing consequences, reflects a legitimate concern for heritage. However, I largely disagree with it, since a blanket prohibition would ultimately harm the very places it aims to preserve.

It is certainly true that insensitive development can do irreversible damage. A single oversized office block can dominate a skyline that has remained largely unchanged for centuries, and the demolition of a period building cannot be undone. Historic quarters also have considerable economic value in their own right, drawing visitors whose spending supports thousands of local businesses. For these reasons, protecting landmarks and the overall character of old districts should be a clear priority for planners.

Yet a complete ban confuses preservation with freezing a city in time. Historic centres have always evolved, with each generation adding buildings of its own era, and many admired streets are the result of such layering. More practically, prohibiting construction where land is most in demand drives up property prices, forces lower-income residents out and leaves the centre dominated by short-term lets and souvenir shops. The outcome is often a district that looks authentic but has lost the everyday life that once defined it.

A more sophisticated approach combines firm protection with carefully managed change. Listed buildings can be safeguarded absolutely, while strict design codes govern the height, materials and scale of anything new. Derelict sites and disused commercial buildings can be converted into homes, bringing residents back without compromising the streetscape. This allows cities to accommodate growth while keeping their historic identity intact.

In conclusion, historic centres deserve robust protection, but an outright ban on new building would sacrifice housing, vitality and affordability for the sake of a static appearance. Intelligent regulation, rather than prohibition, is the better course.
samples.why: Nuanced, fully sustained position · ideas well developed and logically sequenced · cohesion and paragraphing skilfully managed · wide, precise and natural vocabulary · complex structures handled flexibly with no noticeable errors.
